claims.claim: The L2 and L3 loops are stabilized by the tetrahedral coordination of a single zinc ion by C176, H179, C238, and C242.
claims.source: These loops are stabilized by the tetrahedral coordination of a single zinc ion by C176 and H179 of L2 and C238 and C242 of L3.
claims.evidence: This is based on the crystal structure and is established knowledge.

claims.claim: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity.
claims.source: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity, widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum, and a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy (Butler and Loh, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum.
claims.source: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity, widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum, and a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy (Butler and Loh, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy.
claims.source: Removing Zn2+ from DBD causes loss of DNA-binding specificity, widespread changes in the protein NMR spectrum, and a reduction of ~3 kcal mol−1 in the apparent folding free energy (Butler and Loh, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claims.claim: Overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins causes reversible loss of sequence-specific DNA-binding activity of p53.
claims.source: This inherent malleability has also been demonstrated in cells by overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins (metallothioneins) or adding small-molecule Zn2+ chelators, and observing reversible loss of sequence-specific DNA-binding activity and a switch in recognition by an antibody that recognizes native p53 (PAB1620) to one that binds to unfolded/misfolded p53 (PAB240) (Méplan et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous cell-based experiments.

claims.claim: Overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins causes a switch in antibody recognition from PAB1620 (native p53) to PAB240 (unfolded/misfolded p53).
claims.source: This inherent malleability has also been demonstrated in cells by overexpressing Zn2+-chelating proteins (metallothioneins) or adding small-molecule Zn2+ chelators, and observing reversible loss of sequence-specific DNA-binding activity and a switch in recognition by an antibody that recognizes native p53 (PAB1620) to one that binds to unfolded/misfolded p53 (PAB240) (Méplan et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous cell-based experiments.

claims.claim: Many tumorigenic mutations occur in and around the zinc-binding site.
claims.source: Many tumorigenic mutations occur in and around the zinc-binding site and presumably impair this interaction.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 1 and the biophysical data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: R175H is the most common p53 mutation in cancer.
claims.source: The most common p53 mutation in cancer, R175H, is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176 (Figure 1) and dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity (Butler and Loh, 2003; Yu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on mutation frequency data and is established knowledge.

claims.claim: R175H is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176.
claims.source: The most common p53 mutation in cancer, R175H, is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176 (Figure 1) and dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity (Butler and Loh, 2003; Yu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure (Figure 1).

claims.claim: R175H dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity.
claims.source: The most common p53 mutation in cancer, R175H, is immediately adjacent to the zinc-chelating residue C176 (Figure 1) and dramatically weakens metal-binding affinity (Butler and Loh, 2003; Yu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous measurements and confirmed by data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Some cancers inactivate p53 by upregulating metallothioneins and starving wild-type p53 of zinc.
claims.source: Furthermore, there is evidence that some cancers inactivate p53 by upregulating metallothioneins and starving wild-type (WT) p53 of zinc (Mehrian-Shai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Zinc metallochaperones reactivate mutant p53 by shuttling Zn2+ from extracellular sources through the plasma membrane and into cells.
claims.source: By our definition, zinc metallochaperones (ZMCs) reactivate mutant p53 by shuttling Zn2+ from extracellular sources through the plasma membrane and into cells, thereby increasing intracellular Zn2+ concentrations to levels high enough to remetallate mutant p53.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' definition and proposed mechanism.

claims.claim: ZMCs have proven effective for multiple mutants in cell culture and mouse models of cancer.
claims.source: This approach has proven effective for multiple mutants in cell culture and mouse models of cancer (Yu et al., 2014; Blanden et al., 2015; Garufi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data in the current manuscript (Figures 5-9).

claims.claim: Previous attempts to characterize DBD folding thermodynamics lack information regarding zinc-binding affinity of folded and unfolded states.
claims.source: Previous attempts to characterize DBD folding thermodynamics have yielded valuable insight into mechanisms of p53 dysfunction, and have informed drug development efforts, but are ultimately incomplete because they lack information regarding zinc-binding affinity of folded and unfolded states (Bullock et al., 2000; Bullock et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is a critique of previous work supported by citations.

claims.claim: There is disagreement in the literature regarding which mutants are potentially treatable using zinc-based therapies.
claims.source: Furthermore, there is disagreement in the literature regarding which mutants are potentially treatable using zinc-based therapies, likely because of the difficulty of inferring physical mechanisms from complex biological data and lack of a consensus definition regarding what constitutes a zinc-binding mutant (Garufi et al., 2013; Salim et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations showing conflicting results in the literature.

claims.claim: ΔGapo of wild-type DBD is extremely unfavorable at 37°C, indicating that wild-type DBD is intrinsically unfolded in the absence of zinc.
claims.source: The data reveal for the first time that: (i) ΔGapo is extremely unfavorable at 37°C, indicating that wild-type (WT) DBD is intrinsically unfolded in the absence of zinc
claims.evidence: This is based on thermodynamic measurements extrapolated to 37°C (Figure 2D).

claims.claim: DBD has one of the highest zinc-binding affinities of any eukaryotic protein yet reported.
claims.source: The data reveal for the first time that: (i) ΔGapo is extremely unfavorable at 37°C, indicating that wild-type (WT) DBD is intrinsically unfolded in the absence of zinc, and (ii) DBD has one of the highest zinc-binding affinities of any eukaryotic protein yet reported (Kochańczyk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on direct measurement of KZn (Figure 2A) and comparison to literature values.

claims.claim: The unusually large unfavorable value of ΔGapo and the atypically large favorable value of ΔGZn are predicted to nearly cancel each other out at physiological temperature and intracellular zinc concentration.
claims.source: Remarkably, the unusually large unfavorable value of ΔGapo and the atypically large favorable value of ΔGZn are predicted to nearly cancel each other out at physiological temperature and intracellular zinc concentration, causing the overall free energy change of folding to be near zero.
claims.evidence: This is based on the thermodynamic model and energy landscape calculations shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: p53 is poised between folded and unfolded conformations in the cell, with available zinc concentration being a major determining factor.
claims.source: Although p53's instability at 37°C has been previously documented, our modeling emphasizes that p53 is poised between folded and unfolded conformations in the cell, with available zinc concentration being a major determining factor.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the thermodynamic model (Figure 3A) and supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 10).

claims.claim: Mutations that decrease protein stability and mutations that decrease zinc-binding affinity both cause p53 to lose function by a common unfolding mechanism.
claims.source: It further holds that mutations that decrease protein stability (but not zinc-binding affinity) and mutations that decrease zinc-binding affinity (but not protein stability) both cause p53 to lose function by a common unfolding mechanism, and both might be similarly rescued by increasing the concentration of available Zn2+.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the thermodynamic model that is tested experimentally.

claims.claim: Both stability-class and zinc-binding-class mutants might be rescued by increasing the concentration of available Zn2+.
claims.source: It further holds that mutations that decrease protein stability (but not zinc-binding affinity) and mutations that decrease zinc-binding affinity (but not protein stability) both cause p53 to lose function by a common unfolding mechanism, and both might be similarly rescued by increasing the concentration of available Zn2+.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is validated by cell-based and xenograft experiments (Figures 5-9).

claims.claim: 22 of the most prevalent cancer-associated p53 variants were classified into three classes—stability, zinc-binding, or DNA-binding—based on ΔGapo, KZn, and KDNA.
claims.source: As a test, we apply the model to 22 of the most prevalent cancer-associated p53 variants and classify them into three classes—stability, zinc-binding, or DNA-binding—based on (respectively) ΔGapo, KZn, and KDNA, the latter being dissociation constants for binding to a panel of p53 recognition elements.
claims.evidence: This is based on biophysical measurements shown in Figures 3C and 4.

claims.claim: ZMC1 reactivates members of the stability class of p53 mutants in cells.
claims.source: We validate the model by testing whether ZMC1 reactivates members of the stability class of p53 mutants in cells, a category not previously regarded as being amenable to Zn2+ therapy.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by cell viability assays (Table 1), immunofluorescence (Figure 6A), and xenograft experiments (Figure 9).

claims.claim: WT DBD binds Zn2+ with KZn = (1.6 ± 0.3) x 10−15 M at 10°C.
claims.source: Fitting the data to the one-site binding equation yields KZn = (1.6 ± 0.3) x 10−15 M.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by Tyr fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: This is one of the lowest KZn values ever reported, with only one other eukaryotic protein possessing comparable affinity (PDZ and LIM domain protein 1; KZn = 3.2×10−15 M).
claims.source: To our knowledge, this is one of the lowest KZn values ever reported, with only one other eukaryotic protein possessing comparable affinity (PDZ and LIM domain protein 1; KZn = 3.2×10−15 M) (Kochańczyk et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison to literature values.

claims.claim: Full-length p53 binds zinc with KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and Hill coefficient n = 0.99 ± 0.02.
claims.source: Fitting the data to the Hill-binding equation reveals KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and n = 0.99 ± 0.02, indicating that each monomer binds zinc independently and that the isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by Tyr fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Each monomer of the p53 tetramer binds zinc independently.
claims.source: Fitting the data to the Hill-binding equation reveals KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and n = 0.99 ± 0.02, indicating that each monomer binds zinc independently and that the isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the Hill coefficient being approximately 1.

claims.claim: The isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
claims.source: Fitting the data to the Hill-binding equation reveals KZn = (0.4 ± 0.1) x 10−15 M and n = 0.99 ± 0.02, indicating that each monomer binds zinc independently and that the isolated DBD is an accurate representation of the DBD in the full-length p53 tetramer.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similar KZn values and lack of cooperativity.

claims.claim: Unfolded WT DBD binds zinc with KZn,U = (42 ± 7) x 10−9 M.
claims.source: We then measured KZn,U by competition assay between urea-denatured apoDBD and the fluorescent Zn2+ chelator FluoZin-3 (Figure 2B). The apparent KZn,U value of (42 ± 7) x 10−9 M is 107-fold weaker than KZn.
claims.evidence: This is measured by FluoZin-3 competition assay shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: KZn,U of unfolded WT DBD is 107-fold weaker than KZn.
claims.source: The apparent KZn,U value of (42 ± 7) x 10−9 M is 107-fold weaker than KZn.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the measured KZn and KZn,U values.

claims.claim: C176S mutant has KZn,U = (50 ± 23) x 10−9 M, essentially identical to WT.
claims.source: We generated a Ser mutant of the zinc-binding residue C176 and found its KZn,U to be essentially identical ((50 ± 23) x 10−9 M), indicating that the zinc-binding sites in the native and unfolded proteins are distinct (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is measured by FluoZin-3 competition assay shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The zinc-binding sites in the native and unfolded proteins are distinct.
claims.source: We generated a Ser mutant of the zinc-binding residue C176 and found its KZn,U to be essentially identical ((50 ± 23) x 10−9 M), indicating that the zinc-binding sites in the native and unfolded proteins are distinct (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutating a native zinc ligand does not affect KZn,U.

claims.claim: R175H is a pure zinc-binding-class mutant.
claims.source: Plotting folding free energy of DBD vs. [Zn2+]free (10°C) reveals that R175H (green) is a pure zinc-binding-class mutant whereas A138V (red) is a pure stability-class mutant.
claims.evidence: This is shown by the shifted deflection point in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: A138V is a pure stability-class mutant.
claims.source: Plotting folding free energy of DBD vs. [Zn2+]free (10°C) reveals that R175H (green) is a pure zinc-binding-class mutant whereas A138V (red) is a pure stability-class mutant.
claims.evidence: This is shown by the lower y-intercept in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Temperature dependence of apoDBD folding free energy yields ΔHm = 171 ± 20 kcal mol−1, Tm = 300 ± 1 K, and ΔCp = 7.0 ± 1.7 kcal mol−1 K−1.
claims.source: Temperature dependence of apoDBD folding free energy fit to the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) yields ΔHm = 171 ± 20 kcal mol−1, Tm = 300 ± 1 K, and ΔCp = 7.0 ± 1.7 kcal mol−1 K−1 (fit value ± SE of fit).
claims.evidence: This is obtained by fitting temperature-dependent stability data to the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation (Figure 2D).

claims.claim: At 10°C, WT apoDBD is stable even without zinc (ΔGapo = −6.3 kcal mol−1).
claims.source: When the protein is kept cool (10°C) it is stable even without zinc (ΔGapo = −6.3 kcal mol−1; Figure 2D), making Fholo effectively unity at all relevant concentrations of free zinc (>10−15 M; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 3A.

claims.claim: At 37°C, WT apoDBD is completely unfolded without zinc (ΔGapo = 6.9 kcal mol−1).
claims.source: At 37°C, however, the protein is completely unfolded without zinc (ΔGapo = 6.9 kcal mol−1).
claims.evidence: This is extrapolated from temperature-dependent measurements using the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation.

claims.claim: At 37°C and 10−10 M free zinc, WT p53 has Fholo = 0.43.
claims.source: Strikingly, the high zinc-binding affinity of WT apoDBD together with the concentration of free zinc in the typical cell (10−10 M) (Krezel and Maret, 2006; Vinkenborg et al., 2009) result in an overall ΔGfold near zero and Fholo = 0.43 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape model shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Under normal physiological conditions, WT p53 is balanced on the edge of folding and unfolding.
claims.source: This suggests that under normal physiological conditions, WT p53 is balanced on the edge of folding and unfolding and may be pushed in either direction by surprisingly small changes in [Zn2+]free, ΔGapo, KZn, or temperature.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the energy landscape calculations.

claims.claim: Raising [Zn2+]free to 10−9 M yields Fholo = 0.9.
claims.source: For example, raising [Zn2+]free to 10−9 M or lowering it to 10−11 M yields Fholo values of 0.9 and 0.08, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape model.

claims.claim: Lowering [Zn2+]free to 10−11 M yields Fholo = 0.08.
claims.source: For example, raising [Zn2+]free to 10−9 M or lowering it to 10−11 M yields Fholo values of 0.9 and 0.08, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the energy landscape model.

claims.claim: At 10°C, ΔGholo,theory (−12.3 kcal mol−1) and ΔGholo (−10.6 kcal mol−1) are in good agreement.
claims.source: At 10°C, where ΔGapo and ΔGholo are both determined experimentally, ΔGholo,theory (−12.3 kcal mol−1) and ΔGholo (−10.6 kcal mol−1) are in good agreement.
claims.evidence: This validates the model by comparing to previous measurements by Fersht and coworkers.

claims.claim: At 37°C, ΔGholo,theory and ΔGholo are nearly identical (−2.9 kcal mol−1 and −3.0 kcal mol−1, respectively).
claims.source: At 37°C, where ΔGapo and ΔGholo are extrapolated values, ΔGholo,theory and ΔGholo are nearly identical (−2.9 kcal mol−1 and −3.0 kcal mol−1, respectively).
claims.evidence: This validates the extrapolation by comparing to previous measurements by Fersht and coworkers.

claims.claim: The ΔCp value obtained is substantially higher than the figure calculated based on the change in accessible surface area of holoDBD upon unfolding (3.8 kcal mol−1 K−1).
claims.source: We note, however, that the ΔCp value we obtain is substantially higher than the figure calculated based on the change in accessible surface area of holoDBD upon unfolding (3.8 kcal mol−1 K−1) (Bullock et al., 2000; Myers et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to theoretical predictions from structure.

claims.claim: apoDBD possesses a stability that is unusually dependent on temperature owing to its large ΔCp value.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that apoDBD, owing to its large ΔCp value, possesses a stability that is unusually dependent on temperature.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the measured ΔCp value.

claims.claim: 17 of the top 20 most common tumorigenic p53 mutations impair DBD thermodynamic stability, zinc-binding affinity, or both.
claims.source: Of the 22 most common tumorigenic mutations examined here, all but three reduce stability by >1 kcal mol−1, decrease Zn2+ binding affinity by >10 fold, or both. The remaining three belong to the DNA-contact class.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and summarized in the text.

claims.claim: Pure zinc-binding mutants exhibit decreased Zn2+ affinity but normal stability.
claims.source: Pure zinc-binding mutants exhibit decreased Zn2+ affinity but normal stability and thus cluster near a vertical line drawn directly below WT DBD (green box).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Members of the zinc-binding class include R175H, C176S, C242S, and H179R.
claims.source: Members of this class include R175H as well as the direct Zn2+ ligating mutants C176S, C242S, and H179R.
claims.evidence: This is based on the classification shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The analysis reveals a number zinc-binding mutations (P152L, L194F, R282Q) that were not previously suspected due to their long distances from the metal-binding pocket.
claims.source: Significantly, the analysis reveals a number zinc-binding mutations (P152L, L194F, R282Q) that were not previously suspected as being so due to their long distances from the metal-binding pocket (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on the classification in Figure 3C and structural analysis in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Pure stability mutants are less stable than WT but suffer no zinc-binding deficiency.
claims.source: Pure stability mutants are less stable than WT but suffer no zinc-binding deficiency; these are defined by falling near the horizontal line drawn to the left of WT DBD (red box in Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Destabilizing WT apoDBD using sub-denaturing amounts of urea does not affect KZn.
claims.source: To validate that protein stability can indeed be separated from zinc affinity in this manner, we destabilized WT apoDBD using sub-denaturing amounts of urea and measured KZn using the Tyr fluorescence assay. These data (open circles) fall on the horizontal line as predicted by the model.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C (open circles).

claims.claim: The mixed-phenotype mutants (A138V, V267F, R158H, M237I) decrease both stability and zinc affinity.
claims.source: The mixed-phenotype mutants (A138V, V267F, R158H, M237I; orange box in Figure 3C) decrease both stability and zinc affinity.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Only three mutations (R248Q, R273H, R280K) do not impair stability or metal affinity.
claims.source: Only three mutations (R248Q, R273H, R280K) do not impair stability or metal affinity (blue box in Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: R248Q, R273H, and R280K residues are in direct contact with DNA.
claims.source: These residues are in direct contact with DNA (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the crystal structure (Figure 1).

claims.claim: DNA-contact mutants are more stable than WT, likely because they remove or reposition a positive charge and reduce repulsions in the highly cationic DNA-binding groove.
claims.source: DNA-contact mutants are more stable than WT, likely because they remove or reposition a positive charge and reduce repulsions in the highly cationic DNA-binding groove (Butler and Loh, 2003; Bullock et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations.

claims.claim: DNA-contact mutants bind zinc normally.
claims.source: Our data confirm that they bind zinc normally and have lost DNA-binding affinity (vide infra).
claims.evidence: This is confirmed by the data in Figure 3C and Figure 4.

claims.claim: The most severe stability-class mutant reduces ΔGapo by 4.6 kcal mol−1 (E285K).
claims.source: The most severe member of each class reduces ΔGapo by 4.6 kcal mol−1 (E285K) and KZn by 5 orders of magnitude (C176S).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1.

claims.claim: The most severe zinc-binding-class mutant reduces KZn by 5 orders of magnitude (C176S).
claims.source: The most severe member of each class reduces ΔGapo by 4.6 kcal mol−1 (E285K) and KZn by 5 orders of magnitude (C176S).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1.

claims.claim: Several zinc-binding or mixed mutations (L194F, R282Q, V157F, R158H, P152L) lie far from the canonical zinc-binding pocket, suggesting long-range communication between distant regions of DBD.
claims.source: Additionally, several zinc-binding or mixed mutations (L194F, R282Q, V157F, R158H, P152L) lie far from the canonical zinc-binding pocket, suggesting long-range communication between distant regions of DBD.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the structural locations shown in Figure 1 and the biophysical data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Adjacent mutations can produce markedly different effects.
claims.source: The subtle nature of DBD structure and energetics is also evident from the observation that adjacent mutations can produce markedly different effects. For example, R248Q is a classic DNA-contact mutant whereas R249S is a pure zinc-binding mutant.
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing R248Q and R249S in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: R248Q is a classic DNA-contact mutant whereas R249S is a pure zinc-binding mutant.
claims.source: For example, R248Q is a classic DNA-contact mutant whereas R249S is a pure zinc-binding mutant.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Most of the stability and mixed mutants maintain similar binding affinity for the different p53REs.
claims.source: By visual inspection, most of the stability and mixed mutants maintain similar binding affinity for the different p53REs, whereas all of the DNA-contact mutants and most of the zinc-binding mutants lose measurable affinity for all p53REs (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 4.

claims.claim: All of the DNA-contact mutants and most of the zinc-binding mutants lose measurable affinity for all p53REs.
claims.source: By visual inspection, most of the stability and mixed mutants maintain similar binding affinity for the different p53REs, whereas all of the DNA-contact mutants and most of the zinc-binding mutants lose measurable affinity for all p53REs (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The majority of zinc-binding mutants purify with sub-stoichiometric but detectable zinc content.
claims.source: The majority of zinc-binding mutants purify with sub-stoichiometric but detectable zinc content (e.g. R175H contains 0.6 equivalents of Zn2+ 14), and consequently should show partial DNA-binding activity.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous measurements cited in the text.

claims.claim: Loss of DNA-binding in zinc-binding mutants may be caused by Zn2+ misligating to non-native sites.
claims.source: We speculated that the loss of DNA-binding may be caused by Zn2+ misligating to non-native sites (KZn,U = 42 x 10−9 M; Figure 2B) that out-compete the native site at the temperature of protein expression (18°C).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the remetallation experiment.

claims.claim: Removing all bound metal and then remetallating using a EGTA/ZnCl2 buffering system restored measurable DNA-binding affinity to zinc-binding mutants P152L, R175H, H179R, and L194F.
claims.source: To test this hypothesis, we attempted to re-establish native metallation status to the zinc-binding mutants P152L, R175H, H179R, and L194F by first removing all bound metal and then remetallating using a EGTA/ZnCl2 buffering system. This procedure restored measurable DNA-binding affinity (WAF1 oligonucleotide) to all four mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Zinc misligation contributes to loss of DNA-binding activity for the zinc-binding class of mutants.
claims.source: These data suggest that zinc misligation contributes to loss of DNA-binding activity for this class of mutants.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the remetallation experiment results.

claims.claim: P152L maintains WT-like affinity for WAF1 5', GADD45, and RGC, but loses all measurable affinity for PUMA, Type IV collagenase, p53RFP, MDM2, and BAX.
claims.source: P152L maintains WT-like affinity for WAF1 5', GADD45, and RGC, but loses all measurable affinity for PUMA, Type IV collagenase, p53RFP, MDM2, and BAX.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Y220C maintains affinity for WAF1 5', GADD45, PUMA, and Type IV Collagenase, but seems to lose affinity for p53RFP, MDM2, BAX, and RGC.
claims.source: As another example from the stability mutant category, Y220C maintains affinity for WAF1 5', GADD45, PUMA, and Type IV Collagenase, but seems to lose affinity for p53RFP, MDM2, BAX, and RGC.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 4.

claims.claim: E285K gains affinity for all p53REs, but the increase in affinity ranges from threefold for WAF1 5' to 15-fold for MDM2.
claims.source: Additionally, E285K gains affinity for all p53REs, but the increase in affinity ranges from threefold for WAF1 5' to 15-fold for MDM2.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the heat map in Figure 4.

claims.claim: E285K may bind more tightly to all DNA sequences due to enhanced electrostatic interactions with the phosphate backbone afforded by the negative-to-positive charge reversal near the active site.
claims.source: E285K may bind more tightly to all DNA sequences due to enhanced electrostatic interactions with the phosphate backbone afforded by the negative-to-positive charge reversal near the active site.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural location and charge change.

claims.claim: Y163C, Y205C, Y220C, and Y234C are all destabilized (ΔGapo = 3.5–5.0 kcal/mol).
claims.source: Y163C, Y205C, Y220C, and Y234C are all destabilized (ΔGapo = 3.5–5.0 kcal/mol), but, unlike all other members of the stability class except for M237I, their ΔGfold values fail to increase with [Zn2+]free (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—source data 1.

claims.claim: Y234C has KZn = (1.9 ± 0.2) x 10−15 M, similar to WT.
claims.source: First, direct measurement of KZn by Tyr fluorescence yields a value of (1.9 ± 0.2) x 10−15 M for Y234C (Figure 3—source data 1), the only Tyr→Cys mutant that was able to survive the zinc removal procedure without aggregating.

claims.claim: Mutations in six positions (R175, C176, H179, C242, G245, V272) are associated with new cancer cases in more than 120,000 patients each year in the U.S.

Mutations in these six positions alone are associated with new cancer cases in more than 120,000 patients each year in the U.S. (Siegel et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on cancer incidence data cited.

results.result: Wild-type p53 DBD binds zinc with exceptionally high affinity (KZn = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ M for isolated DBD and 0.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ M for full-length p53), representing one of the highest zinc affinities reported for eukaryotic proteins. The monomers bind zinc independently (Hill coefficient n ≈ 1), and the isolated DBD accurately represents the full-length protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C35, C42-C46 are well-supported by direct experimental measurements using tyrosine fluorescence assays (Figure 2A) and comparison to literature values. The Hill coefficient near 1.0 validates independent binding, and the similar KZn values between isolated DBD and full-length p53 support the representativeness of the isolated domain.

results.result: Wild-type apoDBD (zinc-free) exhibits extreme thermodynamic instability at physiological temperature (ΔGapo = +6.9 kcal/mol at 37°C) but is stable at 10°C (ΔGapo = -6.3 kcal/mol). This unusual temperature dependence arises from an anomalously large heat capacity change (ΔCp = 7.0 kcal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). The unfolded protein binds zinc ~10⁷-fold more weakly than the folded protein (KZn,U = 42 nM vs KZn = 1.6 fM), and these binding sites are distinct.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C34, C47-C50, C53-C55, C63, C170-C171 are supported by temperature-dependent urea denaturation experiments (Figure 2D) and FluoZin-3 competition assays (Figure 2B). The extrapolation to 37°C using the Gibbs-Helmholtz equation is validated by agreement with previous work by Fersht and colleagues (C60-C61). However, the ΔCp value is substantially higher than predicted from surface area calculations (C62), which the authors acknowledge but do not fully explain.

results.result: At physiological conditions (37°C, 10⁻¹⁰ M free zinc), wild-type p53 exists in a near-equilibrium state between folded and unfolded conformations (Fholo = 0.43), with available zinc concentration being a major determinant of folding status. This prediction is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments showing comparable PAB240 (unfolded-specific) and PAB1620 (native-specific) antibody binding in wild-type p53 cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37, C56-C59, C154-C155, C172, C192 are supported by the thermodynamic model (Figure 3A) and validated by conformation-specific antibody experiments (Figure 10). The model's prediction that small changes in zinc concentration dramatically affect folding is consistent with the measured thermodynamic parameters. However, the cellular experiments (C155, C192) do not account for potential effects of chaperones, binding partners, or differential antibody affinities, which the authors acknowledge.

results.result: Of the 22 most common tumorigenic p53 mutations characterized, 17 (77%) impair thermodynamic stability, zinc-binding affinity, or both. Mutations classify into distinct categories: pure zinc-binding (e.g., R175H, C176S, C242S, H179R), pure stability (e.g., Y234A, V272M, E285K), mixed phenotype (e.g., A138V, V267F, R158H, M237I), and DNA-contact (R248Q, R273H, R280K). Several zinc-binding mutations (P152L, L194F, R282Q) were identified far from the metal-binding pocket, suggesting long-range structural communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C40, C64-C76, C156, C176 are well-supported by comprehensive biophysical characterization (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1) including urea denaturation at various zinc concentrations and direct zinc-binding measurements. The classification scheme is validated by control experiments (e.g., urea-destabilized WT falls on the stability axis as predicted). DNA-binding assays (Figure 4) confirm functional consequences. The discovery of distal zinc-binding mutations (C67) is particularly significant.

results.result: DNA-binding analysis reveals that stability and mixed mutants generally maintain similar affinity for different p53 recognition elements, while DNA-contact and most zinc-binding mutants lose measurable affinity for all tested sequences. Remetallation experiments restored DNA-binding to zinc-binding mutants (P152L, R175H, H179R, L194F), suggesting zinc misligation contributes to their loss of function. Some mutants show sequence-specific effects (e.g., P152L maintains affinity for some but not all p53REs).
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C89 are supported by fluorescence anisotropy measurements with 10 different p53 recognition elements (Figure 4). The remetallation experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) provides strong evidence for zinc misligation as a mechanism of dysfunction. However, the speculation about E285K's enhanced DNA binding (C89) lacks direct structural evidence. The observation of mutation-specific effects on different p53REs is well-documented but not fully explained by the thermodynamic model.

results.result: ZMC1 treatment successfully reactivates both zinc-binding class mutants (R175H, C176S, L194F) and stability-class mutants (Y234A, V272M) in cell-based assays, as demonstrated by enhanced cell killing (EC50 = 2-10 nM), PAB240-monitored refolding, and restoration of PUMA/NOXA transcription. Notably, the stability mutant V272M shows the lowest EC50 (2 nM), demonstrating that mutations causing only thermodynamic destabilization can be rescued by increasing intracellular zinc.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C41, C102, C107-C108, C111, C116, C124, C131, C135, C142-C144, C165 are strongly supported by multiple complementary assays: cell viability (Figure 5, Table 1), immunofluorescence (Figure 6A), immunoprecipitation (Figure 6B), and RT-PCR (Figure 6C). The reactivation of stability-class mutants is a key validation of the thermodynamic model and represents a novel finding. The consistency across different assay types strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: ZMC1 treatment inhibits tumor growth in mouse xenograft models bearing the stability-class mutant V272M but not the more severely destabilized E285K mutant, providing in vivo validation that zinc metallochaperones can reactivate certain stability-class p53 mutations in addition to zinc-binding mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C151, C153 are supported by xenograft experiments (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1) showing differential tumor growth inhibition. The in vivo validation of V272M reactivation is significant, though the sample sizes and statistical analysis details are not fully specified in the claims. The failure to inhibit E285K tumors is consistent with the severity of its destabilization and provides an important negative control.

results.result: Several mutants fail to respond to ZMC1 treatment despite being classified as zinc-binding or stability class: P152L and R282Q (zinc-binding class) show no enhanced sensitivity, while Y234C and E285K (stability class) fail to refold or regain function. The failure of Y234C is consistent with zinc misligation to the introduced cysteine residue, while E285K's extreme instability (ΔΔGapo = -4.6 kcal/mol) prevents refolding at the zinc concentrations achieved by ZMC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C103, C109-C110, C118, C125, C132, C145-C146, C166 are supported by cell viability assays (Table 1, Figure 5), immunofluorescence (Figure 6A), and immunoprecipitation (Figure 6B). The biophysical explanation for Y234C failure (C110) is well-supported by KZn,U measurements (C94). The E285K result highlights limitations of the approach and is consistent with the thermodynamic model. These negative results are important for defining the scope of ZMC therapy.

results.result: Tyr→Cys mutants (Y163C, Y205C, Y220C, Y234C) represent exceptions to the thermodynamic model: they are destabilized but their folding free energy does not increase with zinc concentration. Y234C binds zinc with near-wild-type affinity in the folded state (KZn = 1.9 fM) but the unfolded state binds zinc twice as tightly as wild-type (KZn,U = 20 nM vs 42 nM), consistent with zinc misligation to the extra cysteine. The Y234A mutant restores the predicted zinc-dependent stabilization, confirming that the cysteine causes the anomaly.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C97, C167 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: zinc-dependent stability measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), direct KZn measurements (C91), KZn,U measurements in urea (C94), and the Y234A rescue experiment (C95, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The mechanistic explanation of zinc misligation is compelling and consistent with all observations. This represents an important caveat to the general model and has implications for which mutants are treatable.

results.result: The mixed stability/zinc-binding mutant M237I shows the greatest decrease in PAB240 staining after ZMC1 treatment, indicating successful refolding, yet cells expressing M237I are insensitive to ZMC1 and the mutant fails to activate transcription of p53 target genes. This disconnect between refolding and function suggests M237I compromises p53 through an additional mechanism beyond thermodynamic instability and zinc binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C130 are supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 6A), immunoprecipitation (Figure 6B), cell viability assays (Table 1), and luciferase reporter assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The observation is reproduced in human cancer cell lines (C128, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, 1E). This result highlights an important limitation of the thermodynamic model: structural integrity of the folded state matters beyond just achieving the folded conformation. The speculation about additional mechanisms (C129) is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Lowering temperature to 22°C for 4 hours synergizes with ZMC1 to enable refolding and functional rescue of the severely destabilized E285K mutant (3.8-fold decrease in EC50), which is refractory to ZMC1 at 37°C. Similar temperature-dependent enhancement is observed for R175H (2.4-fold decrease in H1299 cells), demonstrating that temperature acts synergistically with zinc for both stability-class and zinc-binding-class mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C150 are supported by cell viability assays at different temperatures (Figure 7A-B) and immunofluorescence (Figure 7C). The temperature-dependent rescue is consistent with the thermodynamic model's prediction that both temperature and zinc concentration determine folding. However, the clinical applicability of this approach is questionable, as the authors do not discuss feasibility of systemic hypothermia. The result is scientifically valid but of uncertain therapeutic relevance.

results.result: The thermodynamic model predicts that both stability-class and zinc-binding-class mutants lose function through a common unfolding mechanism and should be similarly rescuable by increasing zinc concentration. Five of eight zinc-binding class mutants and three stability-class mutants were successfully reactivated by ZMC1 in cells. However, discrepancies between biophysical predictions and biological outcomes exist, as the energetic modeling does not account for structural effects, mislocalization, or other cellular factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39, C157-C161 represent the integration of biophysical and cellular data. The core prediction (C38-C39) is validated by the successful reactivation of multiple mutants from both classes. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (C158-C161): some mutants predicted to be rescuable are not (e.g., P152L, R282Q), likely due to structural perturbations or cellular factors not captured by the thermodynamic model. The correlation between biophysical and biological data is good but imperfect, which is honestly reported.

results.result: Based on the frequency of rescuable mutations (R175, C176, H179, C242, G245, V272) and U.S. cancer incidence data, zinc metallochaperones have the potential to treat more than 120,000 patients annually in the United States.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C194 extrapolate from mutation frequencies and cancer incidence statistics to estimate treatable patient numbers. While the calculation is based on cited cancer incidence data (Siegel et al., 2020) and the demonstrated efficacy for specific mutants, this represents a theoretical maximum that does not account for: (1) tumor heterogeneity, (2) additional genetic alterations that might affect response, (3) pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic limitations of ZMC1, (4) potential resistance mechanisms mentioned in C121, or (5) the fact that some mutants in these positions may not respond (e.g., R249M vs R249S). The estimate requires clinical validation.

results.result: The thermodynamic model's extrapolation to 37°C is validated by comparison with previous work by Fersht and colleagues: at 10°C, ΔGholo,theory (-12.3 kcal/mol) agrees well with ΔGholo (-10.6 kcal/mol), and at 37°C the values are nearly identical (-2.9 vs -3.0 kcal/mol). However, the measured ΔCp (7.0 kcal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) is substantially higher than predicted from surface area calculations (3.8 kcal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 provide important validation of the temperature extrapolation method. The agreement with Fersht's data at both temperatures (C60-C61) strongly supports the accuracy of the Gibbs-Helmholtz extrapolation. The discrepancy in ΔCp (C62) is acknowledged but not fully explained—the authors tested different buffers and denaturants to rule out artifacts and found no trend in m-values suggesting non-two-state behavior. The high ΔCp may reflect genuine unusual properties of apoDBD, but this remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: Mutants P152L, E285K, M237I, and R273H show no increase in PUMA or NOXA transcription after ZMC1 treatment, consistent with their lack of functional reactivation. However, Y234C and R282Q show elevated mRNA levels for at least one target gene despite failing to show enhanced cell killing or refolding, suggesting the transcriptional increase is insufficient to induce apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C134, C137-C138 are based on RT-PCR data (Figure 6C). The correlation between transcriptional activation and cell killing is generally good, but the exceptions (Y234C, R282Q) are interesting. The interpretation that increased transcription is insufficient for apoptosis (C138) is reasonable but somewhat speculative—alternative explanations include off-target effects of ZMC1 or partial reactivation insufficient for full function. The data are solid but the mechanistic interpretation has some uncertainty.

results.result: Energy landscape modeling predicts that raising intracellular free zinc from 100 pM to 100 nM increases folded R175H from 0.0028% to 2.8%. V272M, destabilized by 2.0 kcal/mol, is predicted to achieve 2.8% refolding at only 10-20 nM free zinc (the concentration buffered by ZMC1), explaining its high sensitivity to the drug.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 are based on calculations from the energy landscape model (Figure 3A-B). The predictions are mathematically sound given the measured thermodynamic parameters. The prediction for V272M (C141) assumes the mutation doesn't change the enthalpy of unfolding, which is reasonable for a relatively conservative substitution but not directly verified. The model's prediction is validated by V272M's exceptional ZMC1 sensitivity (EC50 = 2 nM, the lowest observed), providing strong support for the quantitative accuracy of the approach.

results.result: Background claims establish that p53 is a critical tumor suppressor with unusual properties: missense mutations in the DNA-binding domain contribute to half of new cancer cases annually, the DBD has low thermodynamic stability (Tm = 32-45°C) and unfolds with a half-time of 9 minutes at 37°C, and the protein contains a zinc-binding site (C176, H179, C238, C242) whose disruption causes loss of function. R175H, the most common p53 mutation, dramatically weakens zinc binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C29 represent established knowledge from the literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the study. The structural information (C17-C19) is based on crystal structure PDB 1TSR. The functional consequences of zinc removal (C20-C24) and the properties of R175H (C26-C28) are well-documented in previous work. These background claims are appropriately supported and provide necessary foundation for the novel findings.

results.result: Zinc metallochaperones (ZMCs) are defined as compounds that shuttle zinc from extracellular sources into cells to remetallate mutant p53. ZMC1 forms a 2:1 complex with zinc, acts as an ionophore, and buffers intracellular free zinc to 10-20 nM. Previous work showed ZMC1 is effective for zinc-binding mutants in cell culture and mouse models, but there was disagreement in the literature about which mutants are treatable, motivating the current comprehensive thermodynamic analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33, C98-C101 provide background on ZMCs and motivation for the study. The definition of ZMCs (C30) is the authors' working definition. The properties of ZMC1 (C98-C99) and its previous efficacy (C31, C100-C101) are supported by citations to prior work. The critique of previous thermodynamic studies (C32) and disagreement in the literature (C33) appropriately motivates the need for the comprehensive approach taken in this manuscript.

results.result: Several zinc-binding or mixed mutations (L194F, R282Q, V157F, R158H, P152L) are located far from the canonical zinc-binding pocket, suggesting long-range structural communication. Adjacent mutations can produce markedly different effects: R248Q is a DNA-contact mutant while R249S is a zinc-binding mutant, demonstrating the difficulty of inferring mechanisms from structure alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 highlight important structural insights from the biophysical characterization. The identification of distal zinc-binding mutations (C77) is supported by the classification in Figure 3C and structural analysis in Figure 1. The R248Q/R249S comparison (C78-C79) is a striking example of how adjacent residues can have completely different mechanisms of dysfunction. These observations emphasize the value of comprehensive biophysical characterization over structure-based predictions alone.

results.result: DNA-contact mutants R273H and R280K show no increased sensitivity to ZMC1, as expected since their DNA-binding defects cannot be ameliorated by zinc. However, R280K cells appear dark (folded) by PAB240 staining while R273H stains brightly, suggesting R273H induces misfolding or aggregation in addition to loss of DNA-binding by direct contact.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C122-C123 are supported by cell viability data (Table 1) and immunofluorescence (Figure 6A). The lack of ZMC1 sensitivity for DNA-contact mutants (C106) serves as an important negative control. The differential PAB240 staining between R280K and R273H (C122-C123) is an interesting observation suggesting mechanistic heterogeneity even within the DNA-contact class. The interpretation that R273H causes misfolding (C123) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Human cancer cell lines expressing p53M237I show variable responses to ZMC1: T98G cells are insensitive, SUM149PT shows partial response (viability plateaus at ~40% at 10 μM ZMC1), and BXPC3 cells expressing p53Y220C are also insensitive. This variability may reflect differences in cellular context, zinc homeostasis, or additional genetic alterations.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C114 are based on cell viability assays with human cancer cell lines (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). The variable response of M237I-expressing lines is consistent with the disconnect between refolding and function observed in transfected cells. The insensitivity of Y220C (C114) is consistent with it being a Tyr→Cys mutant prone to zinc misligation. However, the authors do not fully investigate the basis for the cell line-specific differences, which could reflect genetic background, zinc homeostasis differences, or other factors.

results.result: The human cancer cell line T47D bearing endogenous p53L194F mutation shows refolding after ZMC1 treatment (reduced PAB240 and increased PAB1620 staining) and induction of p53 target genes CDKN1A and PUMA, demonstrating that ZMC1 can reactivate mutant p53 in a native tumor cell context.
results.evaluation: Claims C117 and C136 provide important validation in an endogenous tumor cell line context (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, 1E). The refolding and transcriptional activation in T47D cells supports the therapeutic relevance of the findings beyond transfected cell systems. However, the authors do not show tumor growth inhibition or apoptosis induction in this cell line, which would strengthen the translational implications.

results.result: The temperature-sensitive mutant A138V, used as a positive control, shows a 2-fold decrease in PAB240 pull-down after ZMC1 treatment, confirming that the immunoprecipitation assay can detect ZMC1-induced refolding.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). A138V is an appropriate positive control as it is a well-characterized temperature-sensitive mutant. The 2-fold decrease validates the IP assay's ability to detect refolding, though the magnitude is modest compared to some other mutants. This control strengthens confidence in the IP results.

results.result: Comparison to alternative therapeutic approaches: PhiKan and similar compounds bind to the Y220C cavity with weak affinity (Kd = 1-100 μM) and are specific to a single mutant, offering bio-orthogonality but limited scope. In contrast, zinc-induced stabilization leverages p53's existing high-affinity zinc site (KZn ~ 10⁻¹⁵ M) and can in principle refold any stability-class mutant, but lacks bio-orthogonality.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C164 provide context by comparing ZMC therapy to small-molecule stabilizers like PhiKan. The characterization of PhiKan's properties (C162-C163) is based on cited literature. The comparison (C164) accurately captures the trade-offs: ZMCs have broader applicability but may affect other zinc-dependent processes, while cavity-binding drugs are more specific but limited to particular mutants. This is a fair assessment of the relative advantages and limitations.

results.result: The near-zero folding free energy of wild-type p53 at physiological conditions may explain why missense mutations at nearly every codon position in DBD are associated with cancer: most amino acid substitutions decrease folding free energy, and p53's marginal stability makes it particularly vulnerable to destabilization. DNA-contact mutants can be reliably identified from crystal structure inspection.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C175, C177 provide evolutionary and mechanistic context for p53's unusual mutational spectrum. The explanation (C173) is a reasonable inference from the thermodynamic data, though it remains somewhat speculative. The general principle that substitutions usually decrease stability (C174-C175) is well-established and supported by citation. The observation that DNA-contact mutants are structurally obvious (C177) is validated by the data in Figure 1 and Figure 3C.

results.result: Speculation on biological significance: p53's unusual combination of high instability and zinc affinity may constitute a built-in failsafe mechanism or enable conformational regulation through zinc levels. Previous work showed that fresh medium, metal chelators, and oxidative agents can induce conformational changes in p53, and oxidative stress increases free zinc by oxidizing metallothioneins. The authors speculate that physiologic zinc fluctuations could modulate p53 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C179, C180-C184, C191, C193 are largely speculative about the evolutionary rationale and regulatory implications of p53's zinc-dependent folding. The prior observations (C180-C183) are well-documented and cited. However, the speculation that this represents a regulatory mechanism (C179, C184, C191, C193) lacks direct experimental support. The authors appropriately present these as hypotheses rather than conclusions, but they remain untested. The ideas are plausible and interesting but require future work to validate.

results.result: Context on zinc biology: ~10% of human proteins bind zinc, cytosolic free zinc is in the picomolar range while total cellular zinc is in the hundreds of micromolar, and many proteins are functionally regulated by zinc. Although p53's measured KZn is extremely low (1.6 fM), the effective KZn at 37°C (KZn,eff ≈ KZn × Kapo) is orders of magnitude higher due to apoDBD instability, bringing it into a range where physiologic zinc fluctuations could modulate binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C185-C190 provide important context on zinc biology and explain how p53's effective zinc affinity at physiological temperature differs from the measured value at 10°C. The background information (C185-C188) is well-established and appropriately cited. The concept of effective KZn (C189-C190) is a useful insight that reconciles p53's femtomolar measured affinity with the possibility of physiological regulation. The calculation is sound and helps explain how p53 could be zinc-regulated despite its extremely high affinity.

results.result: Several zinc-binding mutants fail to respond to ZMC1 despite impaired zinc affinity: Hs700T cells (p53R249M) were not sensitive to ZMC1 and the mutant did not refold. Possible explanations include structural distortion of the DNA-binding groove (for R249 mutants adjacent to DNA-contact residue R248), misfolding/aggregation to conformations not amenable to zinc binding, or resistance mechanisms such as overexpression of metallothioneins or zinc exporters.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C105, C119-C121 address failures of zinc-binding mutants to respond to ZMC1. The observations (C104, C119) are supported by cited previous work. However, the explanations (C105, C120-C121) are speculative and not directly tested. The structural explanation for R249 mutants (C105) is plausible given proximity to R248, but no structural data are provided. The speculation about misfolding/aggregation (C120) and resistance mechanisms (C121) are reasonable hypotheses but lack experimental support. These represent important limitations that require future investigation.

results.result: The authors conclude that the discovery that ZMCs can reactivate mutants beyond the zinc-deficient class is a significant finding, expanding the potential therapeutic scope of zinc metallochaperone therapy.
results.evaluation: Claim C169 is the authors' assessment of their work's significance. This evaluation is well-supported by the data showing successful reactivation of stability-class mutants (V272M, Y234A) in cells and in vivo (V272M). The expansion from zinc-binding mutants alone to include stability mutants significantly increases the number of potentially treatable patients, as reflected in the patient number estimates (C7, C194). This represents a genuine advance in understanding which p53 mutants might be therapeutically targetable.
